extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, editors, journalism students, and scholars interested in ethics in photojournalism
extracted.subtask_description: A master's thesis examining the history, current practices, and future trajectory of ethical standards in American photojournalism, with case studies (e.g., Abu Ghraib, Brian Walski) and discussion of institutional and photographer-centric ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful and comprehensive depiction (NPPA preamble)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of the photojournalist is the 'faithful and comprehensive depiction of the subject at hand.' Photojournalists operate as trustees of the public and have responsibility to document society and preserve its history through images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images should reveal truth, expose wrongdoing, inspire understanding, and avoid causing harm through intrusion or manipulation. This statement frames photojournalistic priorities and underpins the NPPA Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accurate and comprehensive in representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be accurate and comprehensive in the representation of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy includes not misrepresenting events or subjects; completeness entails providing sufficient information and context so images are not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist manipulation by staged photo opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist being manipulated by staged photo opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing subjects, PR handlers, or others to create contrived scenes that undermine the authenticity of news photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context and avoid stereotyping; recognize bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Be complete and provide context when photographing or recording subjects. Avoid stereotyping individuals and groups. Recognize and work to avoid presenting one's own biases in the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions, selection, sequencing, and editorial framing must supply context; photographers/editors should actively counteract biases and stereotyped portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat subjects with respect and dignity; protect vulnerable people
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat all subjects with respect and dignity. Give special consideration to vulnerable subjects and compassion to victims of crime or tragedy. Intrude on private moments of grief only when the public has an overriding and justifiable need to see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh public interest against privacy/harm; be sensitive in photographing children, victims, and traumatized people; editorial decisions should consider dignity and potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intentionally contribute to, alter, or influence events
rubrics_metrics.description: While photographing subjects do not intentionally contribute to, alter, or seek to alter or influence events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers should avoid actions that change the scene (e.g., staging, directing people) or that would compromise objectivity; example tensions include whether to help injured people in conflict zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing must maintain integrity of content and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should maintain the integrity of the photographic images' content and context. Do not manipulate images or add or alter sound in any way that can mislead viewers or misrepresent subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-processing allowed only to the extent it does not change editorial content (e.g., minimal color/gray adjustments). Combining, cloning, or removing subjects that alter meaning is prohibited. Case studies (e.g., Brian Walski) illustrate consequences of breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pay or materially reward sources or subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pay sources or subjects or reward them materially for information or participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monetary or material inducements can bias behavior and source reliability; they undermine independence and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept gifts or favors that influence coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept gifts, favors, or compensation from those who might seek to influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflicts of interest and perceptions of compromised independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not intentionally sabotage other journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not intentionally sabotage the efforts of other journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional conduct among journalists preserves access and trust; sabotage harms the profession and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive to ensure public business is conducted in public; defend access
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to ensure that the public's business is conducted in public. Defend the rights of access for all journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for transparency and open access to information and events that affect the public; resist censorship and undue restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop vision through study of psychology, sociology, politics, art
rubrics_metrics.description: Think proactively, as a student of psychology, sociology, politics and art to develop a unique vision and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous learning and broad contextual knowledge improve visual reporting and ethical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for access and diversity of viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive for total and unrestricted access to subjects, recommend alternatives to shallow or rushed opportunities, seek a diversity of viewpoints, and work to show unpopular or unnoticed points of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narrow or repetitive coverage; seek plurality and neglected perspectives to provide fuller context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts from political, civic or business involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid political, civic and business involvements or other employment that compromise or give the appearance of compromising one's own journalistic independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain independence; disclosure or recusal when conflicts exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unobtrusive and humble in dealing with subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to be unobtrusive and humble in dealing with subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize intrusion and respect the lived experience of subjects; unobtrusiveness promotes authenticity and reduces harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the integrity of the photographic moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the integrity of the photographic moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid staging or manipulating the decisive moment; preserve sequences and moments as they occurred unless clearly labeled as constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek counsel, lead by example, and continuously study ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive by example and influence to maintain the spirit and high standards expressed in the code. When confronted with situations in which the proper action is not clear, seek the counsel of those who exhibit the highest standards of the profession. Photojournalists should continuously study their craft and the ethics that guide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mentorship, editorial consultation, and professional codes when navigating borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital manipulation principle (NPPA Statement of Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: As journalists we believe the guiding principle of our profession is accuracy; therefore, we believe it is wrong to alter the content of a photograph in any way that deceives the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerging electronic technologies pose new challenges; the benchmark for allowable electronic changes is fair and accurate reporting. Altering editorial content is a breach; examples include undetectable compositing or removing/adding elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: NYT guideline — genuineness and prohibition on adding/removing/rearranging
rubrics_metrics.description: Images in our pages that purport to depict reality must be genuine in every way. No people or objects may be added, rearranged, reversed, distorted or removed from a scene (except for the recognized practice of cropping to omit extraneous outer portions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cropping to remove extraneous outer portions is accepted; any other compositing or rearrangement that changes scene elements is prohibited and considered deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: NYT guideline — limited adjustments and no posing of news situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustments of color or gray scale should be limited to those minimally necessary for clear and accurate reproduction. Pictures of news situations must not be posed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat digital adjustments like darkroom burning/dodging: minimal, for clarity/reproduction only. Posed news photos must be avoided; staged or contrived photos should be clearly labeled when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: NYT guideline — collages/montages must be unmistakable and captions should acknowledge intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: In the cases of collages, montages, portraits, fashion or home design illustrations, fanciful contrived situations and demonstrations of how a device is used, our intervention should be unmistakable to the reader, and unmistakably free of intent to deceive. Captions and credits should further acknowledge our intervention if the slightest doubt is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creative or illustrative visuals are used, clearly disclose the intervention and avoid any implication that such images are documentary news photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional vs photographer-centric ethics (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics are categorized into institutional ethics (publication policies) and photographer-centric ethics (choices made by photographers during capture through handoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional ethics determine what a publication will publish (taste vs ethics), while photographer-centric decisions include posing, aiding subjects, and darkroom/computer handling. Both levels interact and sometimes conflict (e.g., editorial tolerance vs professional codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical Imperative (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is acceptable for one person should be acceptable for everyone; act according to rules you would universalize (nondiscrimination clause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by asking whether you would make the same editorial choice if subjects differed in gender, age, race, etc. Example: consider whether you would publish a partially nude subject regardless of who the subject is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarianism (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh positives and negatives and maximize the good for the greatest number of people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish gruesome images if the public benefit (e.g., driving safety, exposing wrongdoing) outweighs harm to victims or community sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedonism (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act according to what feels good; decisions justified by pleasure or commercial benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing provocative images purely for sales/entertainment is an example; generally contrasted with public-interest-based ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Golden Mean (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizes compromise: if there is a less intrusive or offensive photo that still tells the story, choose the middle-ground option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek less intrusive alternatives rather than extremes; balance competing values rather than absolutist choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veil of Ignorance (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how you would feel if you were the subject; if uncomfortable, seek a different image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empathy to guide decisions about privacy and dignity; imagine being in the subject's place when deciding to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Rule (ethical philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat subjects as you would like to be treated; love thy neighbor as thyself applied to photography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages consideration of subjects' well-being and dignity in decisions about photographing and publishing images.
